REJB 1999-13880 - Texte
intégral

CITATION: Stein c. Québec
(Tribunal administratif)

Cour
supérieure
(Chambre civile)

CANADA

PROVINCE DE QUÉBEC

DISTRICT DE Montréal

NO : 500-05-045298-989

DATE :  1999-08-05

EN PRÉSENCE DE :

Carol Cohen
, J.C.S.

Barry D. Stein

Petitioner

v.

Tribunal administratif du Québec & Dr. Monique
Gratton-Amyot & Me Robert Cloutier

Respondents

et

Régie de l'assurance-maladie du Québec

Mise en cause

Cohen J.C.S.:-

1
In 1996 and 1997, Barry
Stein underwent two operations in New York City to treat the spread of colon
cancer to his liver. Two years later, no trace of the cancerous lesions on his
liver remained.

2
Stein's claim for
reimbursement of the cost of these treatments from the Régie de
l'Assurance-maladie du Québec (the “Régie”) was
refused on October 8
th
, 1996
and June 10
th
, 1997. He applied
for review of these decisions to the Tribunal Administratif du Québec,
Section des affaires sociales (the “T.A.Q.”), whichmaintained the
Régie's refusals to reimburse, on the grounds that part of the treatment
was available elsewhere in Canada and part was experimental.

3
Stein is therefore asking
this Court for judicial review of the T.A.Q. decision, dated September 11
th
, 1998, in virtue of articles 846 and
following of the Code of civil procedure. The Court must decide whether the
decision is manifestly unreasonable and, if so, whether the matter should be
referred back to the Régie for reassessment or whether the Court should
substitute itsown order for reimbursement of the medical expenses incurred by
Stein in New York.

The facts

4
Stein was 41 years old in
1995 when he was diagnosed with colon cancer. In early January 1996, Dr. Phil
Gordon, an internationally renowned expert in colorectal surgery, operated on
Stein in Montreal, removing a one foot long section of his colon.

5
However, several
metastases of the colon cancer were discovered on Stein's liver. These
cancerous lesions could not be removed at the same time, principally due to
their placement and number as well as the lack of a key piece of equipment
— an intra-operative ultra sound machine.

6
Stein's doctors, however,
strongly recommended that the liver metastases be removed as soon as possible,
once he had recovered sufficiently from the colon surgery but no later than 4
to 8 weeks from the date when these spots had first been detected, in January
1996.

7
Stein therefore expected
the liver surgery to take place no later than the middle of March 1996. In fact,
it was scheduled to be performed by Dr. André Roy at St. Luc Hospital on
three separate occasions between January and April 1996, but to no avail.

8
Each time, due to
hospital overcrowding and the qualification of the liver surgery as
“elective”, Stein was told that the operation was cancelled. The
last time, on April 2
nd
, Stein
testifies that he was sent home after having spent the day lying in a hospital
bed and expecting to be wheeled to the operating room at any moment.

9
Stein therefore found himself
well past the March deadline with no surgery in sight. However, since the
diagnosis of the liver metastases in January, Stein had done extensive research
and consulted various experts as to the treatment which would be advisable for
his condition. All of these doctors, who either examined Stein or viewed his
X-rays and test results, agreed that the spots shouldbe removed as soon as
possible.

10
In particular, Dr. John
Daly of New York, an international expert in liver surgery whom Stein had
consulted in late February, strongly recommended that three treatments be
available when the operation on his liver would be performed.

11
These three treatments
were, firstly, liver resection or cutting of the liver, the procedure
originally scheduled for St. Luc hospital, preferably with the aid of the
intra-operative ultra sound machine; secondly, cryosurgery, or freezing of
parts of the liver which could not be cut out and, finally, the insertion of an
internal pump under the skin, which would continuously inject chemotherapydrugs
directly into the liver in order to prevent further lesions (the
“Infusaid” pump).

12
Only the first of these
treatments, the liver resection, was available in Montreal and the delay
recommended by Stein's doctors for performing the resection had long passed. As
a result, on April 8
th
, Drs.
Gordon and Gerald Batist wrote to the Régie for authorization to refer
Stein to Dr. Daly in New York for treatment.

13
Extracts of their letter
were reproduced by the T.A.Q. in its decision and they read as follows:

Mr. Barry Stein is a patient of
mine in the Oncology Department of the Jewish General Hospital. He is a 41 year
old male who was diagnosed as having colon carcinoma with one liver metastasis
in December of 1995. The metastasis could not be removed at the time of the
original surgery due to its placement. Further investigations detected 3 other
liver lesions.

After discussionswith specialists
in New York (the New York Hospital), Pittsburg (the Falk Clinic), Houston (M.D.
Anderson Cancer Centre) and here, in Montreal (Hospital St. Luc), it is decided
that the patient would benefit most from surgery on his liver. However, due to
the quantity of the lesions and their placement surgery may not be possible in
all cases. At the time of the surgery an additional ultrasoundwill have to be
carried out on the liver itself. If the lesions cannot be removed by
conventional surgery, cryosurgery will have to be performed to freeze the
remaining lesions and a hepatic pump may have to be installed of infuse FUDR. The
chemotherapy will likely consist of alternate infusion via the hepatic pump
and/or 5FU and Leucovorin chemotherapy systemically. As surgical
intraoperativeplacement of the hepatic infusaid pump is not performed in Quebec
or Canada, I am willing to cooperate with the American doctors following the
surgery on giving chemotheray to this patient.

In view of the seriousness of the
disease and the young age of the patient who is father of 3 children, the
procedure has to be done as soon as possible. Otherwise the prognosis
isguarded.

I strongly support the option of
doing the procedure in the States in view of the fact that at present it is not
available in Canada. It is not classified as experimental, however it is very
specialized. There is published evidence of an important benefit to patients of
this kind. Therefore I would request your authorization be granted on an urgent
and compassionate basis forabove mentioned surgery to be carried out by Dr.
John Daly at the New York Hospital as soon as possible. Dr. Daly is the
Chairman of the Department of Surgery and Surgeon in Chief at the New York
Hospital Cornell Medical Centre. Time factor is critical in this case.

14
On April 12
th
, 1996, the Régie wrote to refuse
this request, notwithstanding the recommendation of Stein's treating
physicians. Extracts of this response, signed by Dr. Huguette Vigeant, who had
not examined Stein, are also reproduced in the T.A.Q. decision:

I regret to inform you that the
Régie de l'assurance-maladie du Québec is unable to grant Barry
Stein authorization to be hospitalized outside Canada to receive the following
medical services:

- Resection of colon carcinoma
hepatic metastasis followed by intraoperative intraarterial intrahepatic
chemotherapy with Infusaid pump.

Indeed, such authorization can
only be granted in cases where diagnostic or therapeutic services required by
the condition of the patient are not available or not sufficiently specialized
in Canada. Based on consultations with medical experts, itappears that the
surgery or cryosurgery proposed are available and performed in Canada. In this
matter, we suggest you contact:Dr. Greg McKinnon3330 Hospital Drive N.W.Calgary
(Alberta) T2N 4N1Tel.: (403) 220-6376 Fax: (403) 283-4740

Dr. Robin Fairfull-Smith501 Smyth
Road, K-14 Ottawa (Ontario)K1H 8L6Tel.: (613) 737-8612 Fax: (613) 737-8371

Dr. Steven Gallinger1225-600
University AveToronto (Ontario)M5G 1×5Tel.: (416) 596-4200 Fax: (416)
586-8550

As for intra-arterial
intrahepatic chemotherapy, through lack of multi center double blind randomized
studies, proof has not been made that this therapy improve survival and,
therefore, authorization cannot be granted on that ground.

Should Mr. Stein decide to go
abroad, the Régie will not assume any hospital services, asprovided for
in Section 15 of the Regulation respecting the application of the
Québec
Hospital Insurance Act
.

The fees for professional insured
services will be assessed in accordance with the provisions of
Section 10
of
the
Québec Health Insurance Act
.

15
Dr. Vigeant also spoke
to Stein when he called her in April 1996. During that conversation, according
to Stein's testimony before the T.A.Q., Dr. Vigeant advised him to forget
further surgery and live his remaining days in peace, saying: “You know,
Mr. Stein, maybe you should just accept it. Maybe you should just enjoy your
life and not do anything”.

16
Stein reacted with shock
and disbelief. He decided instead to follow the recommendations of his treating
doctors and went to New York for two operations, the first on April 16
th
, 1996, when Dr. Daly performed the
liver resection followed by traditional chemotherapy in Montreal, and the
second in January 1997, after the traditional chemotherapy nearly killed Stein,
at which time Dalyperformed cryosurgery and installed the Infusaid pump.

17
At the date of the
hearing before the T.A.Q. and indeed before the undersigned, Stein was free of
any recurrence of the liver lesions. Both he and his treating physicians
credited this state of good health to the treatments received from Daly in New
York.

The standard of review

18
It is not contested that
the Superior Court must exercise restraint when reviewing decisions emanating
from a specialized tribunal such as the T.A.Q., section des affaires sociales
1
.
The Court examines the decision with caution and deference and will intervene
only when the evidence, viewed reasonably, is incapable of supporting the
findings of fact or when the Tribunal's interpretation of the legislation is
patently unreasonable
2
.

19
A recent judgment of the
Supreme Court reiterates the rule that the decision must be manifestly
unreasonable before the Superior Court will intervene in virtue of its
supervisory powers
3
. The concept of a decision which is
manifestly or “patently” unreasonable was defined at length by
Justice Cory in 1993, who concludes as follows:

It is not enough that the
decision of the Board is wrong in the eyes of the Court; it must, in order to
be patently unreasonable, be found by the court to be clearly irrational.
4

20
Four years later,
Justice Cory applied this strict test in the case of an arbitration, holding
that the decision was patently unreasonable when the proof retained by the
arbitration board contradicted the conclusions of its majority
5
.

21
The unreasonable
character of a decision can be evident on its face, without the necessity of
examining the file in detail, according to Justice Gonthier in
National Corn
Growers
6
. In the words of the Court of
Appeal, there must be a rationality between the proof retained by an
administrative tribunal and its final decision:

De la même
façon, il doit y avoir une rationalité entre la preuve proprement
dite et ce qu'un tribunal fait dire à cette preuve. Si celui-ci fonde sa
décision sur des énoncés contraires à ce que la preuve
révèle, il y a alors une erreur révisable, à cause
de l'absence de lien rationnel entre la preuve etles conclusions tirées.

En l'espèce,
il y a des prémisses fausses dans une proportion suffisamment importante
pour justifier la révision.
7

22
This rule has its
origins in the judgment of the Supreme Court in
Paccar
, in which Justice
Sopinka wrote:

Reasonableness is not a quality
that exists in isolation. When a court says that a decision under review is
“reasonable” or “patently unreasonable” it is making a
statement about the logical relationship between the grounds of the decision
and premises thought by the court to be true.
8

23
In sum, the Court must
examine whether it was manifestly unreasonable or irrational for the T.A.Q. to
conclude, on the basis of the proof, that the treatments received by Stein in
New York were either available in Canada or of an experimental nature.

The decision of the T.A.Q.

24
The T.A.Q. relied upon
the following sections of the
Act
9
to
refuse coverage of the Stein's New York treatments:

3
. The cost of the
following services rendered by a professional in the field of health are
assumed by the Board on behalf of every beneficiary, in accordance with this Act
and the regulations:

(a) all services rendered by
physicians that are
medically required
;

[...]

10
. A beneficiary is entitled to exact from the Board the reimbursement
of the cost of the insured services furnished to him
outside

Québec

by a professional in the field of health, except the pharmaceutical services
and medications referred to in the third and fourth paragraphs of section 3,
provided that hedelivers to the Board the receipts for the fees paid by him,
and furnishes it with the information the Board needs to justify the payment
claimed.
10

25
The law
and regulations limit the application of article 10 of the
Act
to
services which are not available in Canada. Moreover, article 3 and related
provisions are interpreted to exclude any “experimental” procedures
from the definition of treatment which is “medically required”.

26
Thus, the
T.A.Q. refused coverage of Stein's first operation, the resection, as it was
available in Quebec, being identical to the surgery which was to be performed
in Montreal at St. Luc hospital.

27
As for the
second operation, the T.A.Q. maintained the position outlined in Vigeant's
April 1996 letter, that cryosurgery was performed in three locations elsewhere
in Canada and that the internal Infusaid pump was not standard in Canada and
therefore to be considered an experimental procedure.

28
Two days
of evidence was heard by the T.A.Q., on March 4
th
and 5
th
1998. Along with
the testimony of Stein himself, the T.A.Q. heard four of the doctors who had
treated Stein, including Dr. Daly, as well as two doctors called by the
Régie, Dr. Jacques Jolivet, not himself a surgeon, and Dr. Jamie Dow, a
“médecin-évaluateur”, called toassess whether the New
York treatments fall under the applicable legislation. Neither of these doctors
had ever examined or treated Stein.

29

Nevertheless, the T.A.Q. gave precedence to their conclusions as to the
availability of the treatments, whether they were medically necessary for Stein
and whether they were of an experimental nature, discounting, for reasons which
are not made clear, the recommendations of Stein's treating physicians.

30
As for the
first operation, the T.A.Q. acknowledges that a delay of more than 6 weeks
would be dangerous for Stein, in the unanimous opinion of all of the medical
experts. However, the T.A.Q. goes on to conclude that the Régie was
justified in refusing the April request by Stein's doctors to have the surgery
performed in New York:

(71) Le
requérant représente que son état de santé d'alors
justifiait la démarche entreprise auprès d'un éminent
spécialiste des Etats-Unis et ce, d'autant que s'en étant au
préalable remis aux soins du docteur André Roy,
spécialiste en chirurgie hépato-biliaire et pancréatique
de l'HôpitalSt-Luc, il n'aurait pu obtenir les soins requis par sa
condition dans un délai raisonnable.

(72) Les experts en
oncologie qui se sont prononcés sur la question sont unanimes à
reconnaître que le délai d'intervention en présence de
métastases au foie doit être le plus court possible, ne devant pas
excéder quatre à six semaines de la reconnaissance de leur
apparition.

(73) Si le
requérant invoque l'urgence de sa situation, l'intimée au
contraire, se défend d'avoir tardé à traiter sa demande,
expliquant avoir agi dans un délai raisonnable dans les circonstances
où elle avait à requérir de l'information
spécialisée compte tenu de la nature même de la
requête qui luiétait présentée en regard du traitement
proposé par l'expert de New-York.

31
This
conclusion is not only irrational but has no relation with the proof presented
to the Tribunal. All of the medical witnesses who testified,
as acknowledged
by the T.A.Q. at paragraph 72 above
, recognized that the delay for the
removal of the liver lesions should be as short as possible. All of the
witnesses — Stein and his doctors —
confirmed
the
numerouscancellations of the surgery at St. Luc. Nevertheless, the T.A.Q.
somehow concludes that the Régie acted reasonably, as the first request
for treatment in New York was only made in April, not in January.

32
This flies
in the face of all logic. Stein and his doctors requested treatment in New York
in
April
precisely
because
the surgery was not being performed in
a timely fashion in Montreal and because it was more than 12 weeks since the
liver lesions had been discovered. To maintain that it was reasonable to make
Stein
continue
to wait for surgery in Montreal when thedanger to his
well-being increased daily is irrational, unreasonable and contrary to the
purpose of the
Health Insurance Act
, which is designed to make necessary
medical treatment available to all Quebecers.

33
The T.A.Q.
in its decision seems to confuse the first operation and the second. Moreover,
it mixes the various criteria for coverage set out in the
Act
and related
statutes and regulations, referring to experimental procedures when discussing
the
first
operation, the resection in April of 1996:

(74)
Considérant que l'intervention au niveau du côlon est survenue le
16 janvier 1996 et qu'un nécessaire délai s'impose par la suite
en vue d'une récupération préalable à toute
nouvelle chirurgie, le Tribunal est d'avis que la consultation auprès du
docteur Roy à compter du 6 mars 1996 n'implique pas un
délaidéraisonnable dans les circonstances. Il en retient que
l'expert en oncologie ne semble pas avoir proposé une solution
chirurgicale au patient, ce qui appert de la note du 2 avril 1996, lequel,
dès lors, a choisi de revendiquer d'autres traitements ailleurs à
l'instigation des docteurs Gerald Batist et Philippe H. Gordon, selon leur
lettre adressée àl'intimée le 8 avril 1996.

(75) Le Tribunal
retient donc que le requérant a plutôt opté pour des soins
chirurgicaux dans le contexte précédemment décrit
où il a consulté nombre d'experts au Canada et aux Etats-Unis.

(76) Compte tenu de
ce qui précède, le Tribunal, en dépit de l'apparence au
contraire, ne peut se convaincre que la seule urgence de la situation soit
à l'origine des traitements recherchés à New-York, qui,
pour partie, étaient de nature expérimentale.

(77) Dans la mesure
où il appartenait à celui-ci de démontrer par une preuve
prépondérante son droit à un remboursement de la part de
l'intimée en vertu notamment de l'article 15 du
Règlement
d'application de la Loi sur l'assurance-hospitalisation
, le Tribunal se
doit de convenir, malgré le caractère grave de l'atteintedont il
est porteur, que le requérant n'a pas assumé le fardeau qui lui
incombait sur ce plan alors qu'il a quitté la province pour recevoir des
traitements spécialisés hors pays.

34
These
extracts of the decision are enough for the Court to intervene to review the
decision. But Stein's lawyers alleged many more grounds for revision, some of
which bear mentioning.

35
Firstly,
the T.A.Q. failed to respect the rules of natural justice. It relied upon
hearsay medical evidence, particularly the conversation between Dr. Vigeant and
the various doctors referred to in her April 12
th
letters. In fact, the
T.A.Q. refers to these doctors as “witnesses”, in the same manner
as if they had been called to give
viva voce
evidence.

36
Moreover,
after

taking the case under advisement, the T.A.Q. concludes from the St. Luc
hospital file that Stein's version of the April 2
nd
surgery cancellation is
false, without choosing to call Dr. Roy, his surgeon at St. Luc, to explain
precisely what happened on that day:

(78) Quinze jours
plus tard, soit le 2 avril, il est de nouveau admis à l'hôpital
jusqu'à 19h00. Le médecin-traitant parle d'une réadmission
éventuelle sans aucune explication notée, sauf une allergie à
pseudofedadrine.

(79) La feuille
sommaire est complétée et signée le 18 avril 1996.
À la mention traitement, il est noté ‘médical’
par rapport à ‘chirurgical’ ou
‘obstétrical.’

(80) Le dossier
fait finalement état que le docteur Roy revoit le patient le 22 mai 1996
où il apprend qu'il a «réglé son
problème» à New York le 6 avril. Il est mentionné
que celui-ci est en instance de chimiothérapie adjuvante.

(81) Enfin, le 19
décembre 1996, le requérant consulte encore pour récidive
de métastases à être réinvestiguée.

(82) Le Tribunal
observe du dossier hospitalier qu'il ne confirme pas le témoignage du
requérant quant au report à plusieurs reprises d'une intervention
chirurgicale souhaitée qu'aurait pu effectuer le docteur Roy, faisant
surtout état d'examens spécialisés au cours du mois de
mars 1996, préalables à la suggestion de
traitementsmédicaux.

37
This
conclusion is all the more incomprehensible when one revisits the T.A.Q.'s
description of the
same
operation, earlier in the same decision:

(18) Le
requérant explique par son témoignage avoir décidé
de s'en remettre aux soins du docteur John M. Daly, de New-York, sur la
recommandation de ses spécialistes-traitants, les docteurs Batist et
Gordon, tel qu'explicité dans leur lettre du 8 avril 1996.

(19) En effet sous
les soins du docteur André Roy, spécialiste en chirurgie
hépato-biliaire et pancréatique de l'Hôpital St-Luc,
celui-ci dit n'avoir pu, dans un délai raisonnable, subir une
résection métastatique du foie, l'intervention à ce titre
devant être reportée à diverses reprises entre les mois
dejanvier et d'avril 1996.

38
The
T.A.Q.'s approach to the January 1997 surgery in New York is no more rational
in relation to the proof. Firstly, all of the medical experts acknowledge that
any follow-up surgery had necessarily to be performed by Dr. Daly, insofar as
he had performed the first operation. The logical conclusion would be that this
surgery would take place in New York, and should be covered by the
Act
,
as the first operation had not been sufficient to remove Stein's liver lesions.

39
Moreover,
by January 1997, Stein not only had
more
lesions on his liver but had
shown an absolute intolerance to traditional forms of chemotherapy. The
only

choice for Stein was the cryosurgery, followed by the insertion of the Infusaid
pump for local chemotherapy. It is admitted by all parties that these
treatments were not available together anywhere in Canada.

40
But is the
Infusaid pump to be considered an “experimental” procedure, as the
T.A.Q. and the Régie maintain? Dr. Daly categorically states that it is
a standard procedure in all cancer centres across the United States. The
Régie's doctor acknowledges that he is aware of the procedure, has
observed it and that it is not available in Canada because of the
cost
of
the pump.

41

Nevertheless, the T.A.Q. concludes that it must be experimental because it is
not known in the Canadian medical community and because there is no Canadian
standard for the procedure.

(61) Or, il ressort
de la preuve présentée qu'à tout le moins en ce qui a
trait à l'implantation de la pompe ‘infusaid’, une telle
technique, si pratiquée de façon routinière par certains
intervenants dans les grands centres américains, n'est pas pour autant
reconnue par l'ensemble de la communautémédicale.

(62) Le docteur
Jolivet, expert de l'intimée, s'est livré sur ce sujet
après avoir étudié la doctrine proposée, se
référant à des études spécialisées
sur l'incidence du traitement de chimiothérapie dont a
bénéficié le requérant à New York sur
unepossible récupération et quant au taux de survie

(63) Le docteur
Jolivet, constatant le nombre limité de patients visés par les
études, déclare ne pouvoir en dégager la conclusion qu'une
chimiothérapie administrée dans une telle condition constitue un
traitement standard.

(64) Le Tribunal
retient l'opinionprécitée quant au caractère
expérimental du traitement administré à l'aide de
l'installation d'une pompe sous-cutanée intra-artérielle.

42
On this
basis,
every
procedure which is not performed in Canada would be experimental,
as it would necessarily be “unknown” to the Canadian medical
community. This is irrational, as there can be no Canadian
“standard” for a procedure which is not performed here. To conclude
otherwise imposes a tautology that will prevent the coverage of
all

proceduresperformed regularly elsewhere but not within the country.

43
Stein
needed surgery on his liver in a timely fashion. Between January and April
1996, he could not get that surgery in Montreal. The subsequent treatments,
which are not available here, saved or at least prolonged Stein's life. These
facts are uncontradicted. To refuse coverage in these circumstances is patently
unreasonable and the Court therefore intervenes to annul the T.A.Q.'sdecision.

44
Finally,
although the Court has sympathy for Stein's plight and the treatment of his
claim for coverage until now, the undersigned is not in a position to replace
the T.A.Q. refusal with a monetary condemnation against the Régie. In
the circumstances, the Régie is to be ordered to accept Stein's claim
for coverage and reasses its value in accordance with the law andregulations.

For all of the Foregoing Reasons, The
Court:

45

GRANTS

Petitioner's Motion in evocation;

46

DECLARES

that the decision rendered by the Tribunal administratif du Québec on
September 11, 1998 is patently unreasonable;

47

ANNULS

the decision rendered by the Tribunal administratif du Québec on
September 11, 1998;

48

ORDERS

the mise en cause Régie de l'assurance-maladie du Québec to
accept Petitioner's claims for coverage for the operations dated April 16, 1996
and January 8, 1997 in New York city and to assess the value of these claims in
accordance with the law and regulations;

49

THE
WHOLE
, with costs against the Respondent and the Mise-en-cause.

Cohen J.C.S.

Mtre Louis G. Brunet
, for Petitioner.

Mtre Michael O'Neil
, for Régie de l'assurance-automobile du
Québec.

Mtre Ovila Chrétien
, for the Tribunal administratif du
Québec.
